prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- President George W. Bush called India's prime minister Thursday to push a proposed nuclear partnership that sparked an unsuccessful no-confidence vote against the Indian leader this week, a White House spokesman said. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh won a confidence vote despite opposition to the nuclear deal. "Both leaders expressed their desire to see the U.S.-India Civil Nuclear issue move forward as expeditiously as possible," Gordon Johndroe said. The phone call took place two days after Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh narrowly survived the no-confidence vote in the lower house of Parliament. The vote was sparked by concerns from the opposition that India was kowtowing to the U.S. The tentative deal was announced in 2006 and signed by Bush and Singh a year ago. Under the agreement, which will need to be approved by the U.S. Congress, India would have access to U.S. nuclear fuel and technology for its civilian nuclear power plants. That would happen even though New Delhi, which tested nuclear weapons in 1974 and 1998, has declined to join international non-proliferation agreements. In return, India has promised that it would not transfer the fuel and equipment to its weapons program, and it would allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to inspect at least 14 of its 22 nuclear plants. The plan would also expand U.S.-Indian cooperation in energy and satellite technology. The plan was approved by India's Cabinet last year, and does not have to be ratified by the parliament. The leaders of India's two communist parties -- which hold about 60 seats in Parliament -- have accused Singh of surrendering India's sovereignty to the United States with the deal. A no-confidence vote would have forced Singh to resign, and required the government to hold early elections unless a new coalition could have been formed. The Congress Party-led coalition has governed India since 2004. Tuesday's 275-256 vote was so crucial to the survival of Singh's government that five members of parliament serving prison sentences were freed to cast votes -- under the watchful eyes of their jailers. Shortly after Singh survived the vote, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino praised the deal as "a good one for everybody." "It's good for India because it would help provide them a source for energy that they need, one that is nonpolluting and one that doesn't emit greenhouse gas emissions," she said. "And we think that we can move forward with this. If their legislature lets it move forward, then we can do the same here and then we'll be able to get this wrapped up."

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — President George W. Bush spoke by telephone with Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on Thursday to encourage progress on a proposed civilian nuclear agreement that had triggered an unsuccessful attempt to bring down Singh’s government earlier in the week, according to a White House spokesman.

“Both leaders expressed their desire to see the U.S.-India Civil Nuclear issue move forward as expeditiously as possible,” Gordon Johndroe said.

The conversation came two days after Singh narrowly survived a confidence vote in the lower house of India’s Parliament. Opponents of the nuclear agreement had prompted the vote, arguing that India was being overly submissive to the United States.

The preliminary accord was unveiled in 2006 and signed by Bush and Singh a year ago. If approved by the U.S. Congress, it would give India access to American nuclear fuel and technology for civilian power facilities.

That access would be granted even though India— which conducted nuclear weapons tests in 1974 and 1998—has refused to join international nuclear nonproliferation treaties.

In exchange, New Delhi has pledged not to divert the fuel or equipment to its nuclear weapons program. India would also permit the International Atomic Energy Agency to inspect at least 14 of the country’s 22 nuclear facilities.

The proposal would additionally broaden cooperation between the United States and India in energy and satellite technology.

India’s Cabinet approved the arrangement last year, and parliamentary ratification is not required.

Leaders of India’s two communist parties, which control roughly 60 parliamentary seats, have charged that Singh is giving up national sovereignty to the United States through the agreement.

Had Singh lost the confidence vote, he would have been required to step down. Early elections would then have been necessary unless another governing coalition could be assembled. The coalition headed by the Congress Party has ruled India since 2004.

Tuesday’s vote, which Singh won 275-256, was considered so important to his government’s survival that five imprisoned members of Parliament were released to participate, accompanied and closely monitored by their jail guards.

Soon after Singh prevailed, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino described the agreement as “a good one for everybody.”

“It’s good for India because it would help provide them a source for energy that they need, one that is nonpolluting and one that doesn’t emit greenhouse gas emissions,” she said. “And we think that we can move forward with this. If their legislature lets it move forward, then we can do the same here and then we’ll be able to get this wrapped up.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about President George W. Bush urging Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to advance the U.S.-India civilian nuclear agreement after Singh survived a no-confidence vote.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t replicate CNN’s exact style, but here’s a neutral cable-news-style report:

**Bush urges India to move ahead with landmark nuclear deal**

**WASHINGTON (July 2008)** — President George W. Bush has urged Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to advance a landmark civilian nuclear agreement between the United States and India after Singh’s government survived a crucial no-confidence vote.

Bush spoke by telephone with Singh following the parliamentary vote, congratulating him on the victory and emphasizing the importance of completing the remaining steps needed to implement the accord.

Singh’s coalition won the confidence vote by 275 votes to 256, overcoming opposition from communist parties and other critics who argued that the agreement would draw India too closely into Washington’s strategic orbit.

The deal would give India access to U.S. civilian nuclear fuel and technology despite New Delhi’s refusal to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. In exchange, India has agreed to place designated civilian nuclear facilities under international safeguards.

Before the agreement can take effect, India must secure approval from the International Atomic Energy Agency and a waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The pact would then require final approval by the U.S. Congress.

Supporters say the agreement could help India meet its rapidly growing energy needs and strengthen ties between the world’s two largest democracies. Opponents contend that it could weaken global nonproliferation rules because India has developed nuclear weapons outside the treaty framework.

The parliamentary victory removed one of the biggest political obstacles facing Singh, but both governments faced a tight timetable to complete the international and legislative approval process before Bush left office in January 2009.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the political controversy surrounding the 2008 U.S.-India civil nuclear deal, including the parliamentary confidence vote, opposition from communist parties, and the agreement’s key provisions.
counterfactuals.output:
The 2008 U.S.–India civil nuclear deal was politically contentious because it ended India’s long nuclear isolation without requiring it to join the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), but critics argued that it tied India too closely to U.S. strategic and non-proliferation policy.

### Parliamentary crisis and confidence vote

Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) depended on outside support from communist parties, especially the Communist Party of India (Marxist). The Left parties opposed moving forward with the deal and withdrew support in July 2008, depriving the government of its parliamentary majority.

The UPA then secured support from the Samajwadi Party and sought a confidence vote in the Lok Sabha. On **22 July 2008**, the government survived by **275 votes to 256**. The vote was marred by allegations of bribery and defections; three opposition MPs displayed bundles of cash in Parliament, claiming they had been offered money to support the government. The episode became known as the “cash-for-votes” controversy.

### Why communist and other parties opposed it

The communist parties argued that the agreement:

- Drew India into a broader strategic partnership with the United States and weakened its traditionally independent foreign policy.
- Could constrain India’s ability to conduct future nuclear weapons tests.
- Made Indian policy vulnerable to U.S. domestic legislation, particularly the **2006 Hyde Act**, which allowed Washington to end cooperation under certain circumstances.
- Undermined sovereignty by placing civilian nuclear facilities under permanent international safeguards.

The Bharatiya Janata Party also opposed the final agreement, despite having initiated closer nuclear engagement with Washington while in government. It argued that the terms could restrict India’s strategic nuclear program and did not provide sufficiently firm guarantees on fuel supplies and testing.

### Key provisions

Under the deal and related international arrangements:

- India agreed to separate its **civilian and military nuclear facilities**.
- Designated civilian reactors were placed under **International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards**, generally on a permanent basis.
- The United States and other countries could sell India civilian nuclear fuel, reactors, and technology, even though India had not signed the NPT.
- India retained its nuclear weapons program and was not required to sign the NPT or the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.
- The United States offered fuel-supply assurances and accepted, subject to additional arrangements, India’s right to reprocess U.S.-origin spent fuel.
- U.S. law and the bilateral “123 Agreement” preserved provisions for terminating cooperation—and potentially seeking the return of transferred materials—if India conducted another nuclear test or violated non-proliferation commitments.
- India subsequently obtained an India-specific safeguards agreement from the IAEA and, in September 2008, a waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group allowing global civilian nuclear commerce with India.

Supporters described the deal as recognition of India as a responsible nuclear power and a way to expand energy supplies. Opponents saw it as an unequal bargain that risked limiting strategic autonomy and aligning India too closely with the United States.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a news article explaining Bush and Singh’s phone call about nuclear cooperation, why the deal was controversial in India, and what each country stood to gain.
counterfactuals.output:
# Bush, Singh Reaffirm Nuclear Cooperation as Indian Opposition Intensifies

**NEW DELHI/WASHINGTON** — U.S. President George W. Bush and Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh used a telephone call to reaffirm their commitment to a landmark civil nuclear cooperation agreement, even as the deal faced intense political resistance in India.

The agreement sought to end India’s decades-long isolation from global nuclear commerce. Under its terms, India would separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities and place designated civilian reactors under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards. In return, the United States would revise its laws and work to secure international approval allowing India to buy civilian nuclear fuel, reactors and technology.

The initiative required several steps, including an India-specific safeguards agreement with the IAEA, an exemption from the Nuclear Suppliers Group and approval by the U.S. Congress.

For Singh, the call underscored the strategic importance his government attached to the pact. India’s fast-growing economy needed additional sources of electricity, while domestic uranium shortages had limited the operation of some reactors. Access to foreign fuel and technology promised to expand nuclear generation and free India from restrictions imposed after its 1974 nuclear test.

The deal was nevertheless deeply controversial in New Delhi. Communist parties supporting Singh’s coalition argued that it would draw India too closely into the American strategic orbit and weaken the country’s independent foreign policy. They also objected to provisions in U.S. law—particularly the Hyde Act—that they feared could affect cooperation if India tested another nuclear weapon or adopted policies opposed by Washington.

The opposition Bharatiya Janata Party raised a different set of concerns, arguing that the agreement could constrain India’s nuclear weapons program without formally recognizing the country as a nuclear-weapon state. Critics also questioned whether imported reactors would be too expensive and whether international inspections would compromise national sovereignty.

Singh’s government maintained that India had preserved its strategic autonomy. Military facilities would remain outside safeguards, officials said, while civilian facilities opened to inspection would gain access to the international market.

Washington also had much to gain. The agreement promised to transform relations with a major Asian power after decades of Cold War mistrust. It opened potential opportunities for American reactor manufacturers and nuclear-fuel suppliers, while advancing a broader U.S. goal of building a closer strategic partnership with India.

Bush administration officials also argued that bringing much of India’s civilian nuclear sector under permanent international monitoring would strengthen nonproliferation efforts. Critics in the United States countered that making an exception for India—a country that had never joined the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty—could weaken global rules and encourage other states to demand similar treatment.

The Bush-Singh conversation therefore concerned more than energy. For India, the pact offered international recognition, access to nuclear commerce and a closer relationship with the United States. For Washington, it offered commercial prospects and a durable partnership with one of Asia’s largest powers. The political struggle surrounding it reflected the same reality: the agreement represented a major shift in India’s foreign policy and in the global nuclear order.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Manmohan Singh’s narrow 275-256 confidence-vote victory and how it affected efforts to secure approval of the proposed U.S.-India nuclear partnership.
counterfactuals.output:
On July 22, 2008, Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s government survived a confidence vote in the Lok Sabha by 275 votes to 256. The vote was forced after communist parties withdrew support from Singh’s United Progressive Alliance over the proposed U.S.-India civil nuclear agreement. Singh prevailed with crucial backing from the Samajwadi Party and several smaller parties and independents, although the debate was marred by allegations of vote-buying after opposition lawmakers displayed bundles of cash in Parliament.

The victory removed the main domestic political barrier to the nuclear partnership. It allowed Singh’s government to proceed with the agreement’s remaining international approvals:

- an India-specific safeguards agreement at the International Atomic Energy Agency;
- a waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group, permitting nuclear trade with India despite its status outside the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty;
- final approval by the U.S. Congress.

The margin demonstrated that the deal remained controversial and that Singh’s coalition was politically vulnerable, but it also strengthened his authority to press ahead. The IAEA approved the safeguards agreement in August, the Nuclear Suppliers Group granted a waiver in September, and the U.S. Congress approved the agreement in October 2008.

The partnership ultimately ended India’s decades-long isolation from much of the international civilian nuclear market, giving it access to foreign nuclear fuel and technology in exchange for placing designated civilian facilities under international safeguards.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an international news story set in New Delhi describing the White House response to India’s confidence vote and outlining the civilian nuclear deal’s safeguards, benefits, and remaining approval process.
counterfactuals.output:
**White House welcomes India confidence vote, urges progress on nuclear accord**

**NEW DELHI, July 23, 2008** — The White House welcomed the Indian government’s victory in a parliamentary confidence vote, saying the result cleared a major political hurdle for a landmark civilian nuclear agreement between India and the United States.

Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s coalition survived Tuesday’s vote by 275 votes to 256 after weeks of political turmoil over the accord. India’s communist parties withdrew support for the government, arguing that the deal would draw New Delhi too closely into Washington’s strategic orbit.

The White House said the vote demonstrated India’s determination to move ahead with the agreement and pledged to work with New Delhi and the U.S. Congress to complete the remaining steps. President George W. Bush’s administration has portrayed the pact as a centerpiece of a closer relationship between the two democracies.

The agreement would end more than three decades of nuclear isolation for India, which tested nuclear weapons in 1974 and 1998 and remains outside the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Under the plan, India would separate its civilian and military nuclear programs and place designated civilian reactors and facilities under permanent safeguards administered by the International Atomic Energy Agency. Military installations and material connected to India’s weapons program would remain outside those inspections.

India has also pledged to continue its voluntary moratorium on nuclear testing, strengthen controls on sensitive nuclear exports and support international efforts to prevent the spread of enrichment and reprocessing technologies. A separate safeguards agreement would allow the IAEA to verify that imported nuclear fuel and technology are used for peaceful purposes.

In return, India would gain access to foreign nuclear fuel, reactors and technology. Supporters say that could help meet the country’s rapidly growing electricity needs, reduce dependence on coal and imported oil, and open a potentially lucrative market for U.S. and other foreign nuclear companies.

Critics contend that allowing nuclear commerce with a state outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty weakens global rules and could indirectly assist India’s weapons program by freeing domestic uranium for military use. They have also questioned what would happen if India conducted another nuclear test.

The parliamentary vote does not itself put the accord into effect. India must first secure approval of its safeguards agreement from the IAEA’s Board of Governors. It must then obtain an exemption from the 45-nation Nuclear Suppliers Group, whose guidelines normally restrict trade with countries that do not accept comprehensive safeguards over all nuclear facilities.

After those steps, the U.S.-India bilateral cooperation agreement — known as a “123 agreement” after the relevant section of U.S. atomic energy law — must return to the U.S. Congress for final approval.

With the Bush administration nearing the end of its term, officials face a tight timetable to complete the international reviews and secure congressional action.
